# Anorectal abscess and fistula

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Gastrointestinal disorders > Anorectal abscess and fistula*

[Original Article Link](/library/b30HSf)

---

## Summary

<u>Anorectal abscesses</u> are acute <u>purulent</u> collections in the perirectal area, which can progress to form <u>fistulas</u>. An <u>anal fistula</u> is a ductal connection between the <u>epithelium</u>-lined anorectal lumen and the perianal <u>skin</u>. <u>Anorectal abscesses</u> are most commonly caused by obstruction of the <u>anal gland</u> and consequent bacterial overgrowth. Less common causes include <u>Crohn disease</u>, <u>gastrointestinal infections</u> (e.g., <u>diverticulitis</u>), or <u>malignancy</u>. Clinical features of <u>anal abscesses</u> include anorectal <u>pain</u>, a palpable mass, and signs of <u>cellulitis</u> or systemic infection (e.g., <u>fever</u>). Patients with <u>anal fistulas</u> may present with rectal drainage or drainage from a visible site on the perianal <u>skin</u>. <u>Anorectal abscesses</u> and <u>fistulas</u> are <u>clinical diagnoses</u>. Imaging studies such as CT, <u>MRI</u>, or <u>endosonography</u> are sometimes indicated to assess occult <u>abscesses</u> or complex <u>fistulas</u>. Definitive management requires surgical intervention. <u>Abscesses</u> are <u>incised</u> and drained, followed by <u>open wound</u> healing, while the standard treatment for <u>anal fistulas</u> is fistulotomy.

---

## Epidemiology

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (2:1)

* Age: mean of 40 (range between 20 and 60 years)

* <u>Incidence</u>

* ∼ 100,000 people per year in the US

* ∼ 50% of patients with <u>anorectal abscess</u> develop <u>fistulas</u>.




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* Most common cause: flow obstruction and infection of the anal crypt glands (90% of cases)

* Less common causes

* <u>Chronic inflammatory bowel disease</u> (<u>IBD</u>): <u>Crohn's disease</u>, <u>ulcerative colitis</u> (less commonly)

* Acute infections of the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u>: e.g., <u>complicated diverticulitis</u>, <u>acute appendicitis</u>

* Radiation-induced <u>proctitis</u>

* <u>Iatrogenic</u>

* Foreign body

* <u>Malignancy</u>: e.g., <u>colorectal cancer</u>

---

## Classification

<u>Anorectal abscesses</u> and <u>fistulae</u> may be classified according to their variations in <u>anatomical position</u> and distribution.




### <u>Abscesses</u>




* Perianal (subcutaneous): most common 

* <u>Abscess</u> beneath the perianal <u>skin</u>

* Does not transverse the external sphincter

* Ischiorectal: <u>abscess</u> below the <u>levator ani muscle</u>

* Intersphincteric: <u>abscess</u> between the internal and external sphincters

* Supralevator (least common): <u>abscess</u> above the <u>levator ani muscle</u>





![Anal abscess](media/pvdkmz4aowrll85rvmqaxjtw.jpg)

Anal abscess




### <u>Fistulas</u> (Park's classification)




* Intersphincteric (Park's Type I) 

* Course: along the anatomical space between the internal and external sphincter

* Opening: perianal <u>skin</u> (<u>anoderm</u>) and/or <u>rectum</u>

* Transsphincteric (Park's Type II) 

* Course: penetrates the external sphincter ani muscle into the <u>ischiorectal fossa</u>

* Opening: perianal <u>skin</u> (<u>anoderm</u>)

* Suprasphincteric (Park's Type III) 

* Course: ascends cranially within the intersphincteric space, penetrates the <u>levator ani muscle</u> and follows <u>caudally</u> towards the <u>ischiorectal fossa</u>

* Opening: perianal <u>skin</u> (<u>anoderm</u>)

* Extrasphincteric (Park's Type IV) 

* Course: from the internal opening of the rectal ampulla (<u>above the dentate line</u>) through the <u>levator ani muscles</u>

* Opening: perianal <u>skin</u>

* Subcutaneous/subanodermal/<u>submucosal</u> 

* Course: beneath the perianal/anal <u>skin</u>/rectal <u>mucosa</u>

* Opening: perianal <u>skin</u> (<u>anoderm</u>)/<u>anal canal</u>/<u>rectum</u>





![Anal fistula](media/f6l5svqg6itydnv5if5glivk.jpg)

Anal fistula

## Clinical features

### <u>Abscesses</u>




| <br>Clinical features of <u>anorectal abscesses</u> [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[3]](/library/70a4hQ)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Local symptoms | Systemic symptoms (e.g., <u>fever</u>, chills) | Examination findings |
| Perianal | <br>* Perianal <u>pain</u> and <u>pruritus</u><br><br> | <br>* Typically none<br><br> | <br><br>* Localized <u>erythema</u> and swelling<br><br>* Painful subcutaneous mass, induration, and <u>fluctuance</u><br><br><br> |
| Ischiorectal | <br>* Localized buttock <u>pain</u> and tenderness<br><br> | <br>* Sometimes<br><br> | <br>* Indurated mass in the buttocks<br><br> |
| Intersphincteric | <br>* Rectal pressure and <u>pain</u><br><br> | <br>* Sometimes<br><br> | <br><br>* Tender rectal mass on <u>digital rectal exam</u><br><br>* Occasionally, anal drainage(bloody, <u>purulent</u>, or mucoid)<br><br><br> |
| Supralevator | <br>* Perianal, rectal, and/or buttock <u>pain</u><br><br> | <br>* Usually<br><br> | <br>* Tender rectal mass sometimes palpable on rectal or <u>pelvic exam</u><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Anorectal <u>pain</u> is often exacerbated with sitting and defecation, which can lead to <u>constipation</u>. [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




> [!WARNING]
> Deep <u>abscesses</u> (e.g., supralevator) may manifest with systemic symptoms (e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>signs of sepsis</u>), but few or no localized findings on <u>physical exam</u>. [[3]](/library/70a4hQ)




![Anal abscess](media/yitewz0ldixl8fp6jocpzq93.jpg)

Anal abscess




### <u>Fistulas</u> [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[3]](/library/70a4hQ)




* Continuous or intermittent <u>purulent</u> drainage from the <u>anal canal</u> or perianal <u>skin</u>

* <u>Pain</u> during defecation  [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Examination may reveal a <u>fistula</u> tract in the <u>perineum</u> or <u>anal canal</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> Consider <u>Fournier gangrene</u> in patients with signs of extensive <u>cellulitis</u> and/or <u>necrotic</u> tissue. [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




![Anal fistula](media/an20sqlrz0se05b3mcx24pwg.jpg)

Anal fistula

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)




* <u>Anorectal abscess</u> and <u>fistula</u> are <u>clinical diagnoses</u> (see “Clinical features”).

* Perform perianal inspection and <u>digital rectal examination</u>.

* Consider <u>anoscopy</u> or <u>proctoscopy</u> as needed. [[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)

* Consider <u>MRI</u>, CT, or <u>endosonography</u> if the diagnosis is uncertain.

* Consider <u>septic workup</u> and investigations for the underlying condition (e.g., endoscopy for <u>IBD</u>) as needed.





> [!TIP]
> Ensure adequate <u>pain control</u> and consider examination under sedation or <u>general anesthesia</u> in patients with intense <u>pain</u>. [[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid probing <u>fistulas</u> outside of operative settings to prevent creating new tracts. [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




### Imaging [[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)[[5]](/library/HDWKfn0)




* Indications

* <u>Confirmatory testing</u> for occult <u>abscesses</u>

* Recurrent or complex <u>anal fistula</u>

* <u>Immunosuppression</u>

* Known or suspected anorectal <u>Crohn disease</u>

* Modalities

* <u>MRI</u> <u>pelvis</u> with and without IV contrast: preferred  [[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)

* CT <u>pelvis</u> with IV contrast: may be used in the acute setting [[5]](/library/HDWKfn0)

* Anorectal <u>endoscopic ultrasound</u>





### Additional studies [[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)[[6]](/library/OwWIQn0)




* <u>Septic features</u>: Perform <u>septic workup</u>.

* Workup of underlying disorders: Consider individually; not routinely required.

* <u>Diabetes screening</u>

* <u>HIV screening</u> and evaluation for other <u>immune deficiencies</u>

* <u>Evaluation for Crohn disease</u> (e.g., endoscopy)

---

## Treatment

### <u>Abscesses</u> [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)




#### <u>Incision and drainage</u> [[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)




Drainage is typically performed within 24 hours of presentation.




* Bedside: can be performed by generalists using <u>local anesthesia</u> or <u>procedural sedation</u>  [[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)

* Indications

* <u>Perianal abscess</u>

* <u>Superficial</u> ischiorectal <u>abscess</u>

* Procedure: See “<u>Abscess incision and drainage</u>.”

* Operative: requires <u>surgery</u> consult and <u>general anesthesia</u>

* Indications [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)

* Deep <u>abscesses</u>

* Associated <u>fistula</u>

* <u>Sepsis</u>

* Significant comorbid <u>risk factors</u> (e.g., <u>diabetes</u>, <u>immunosuppression</u>)

* Procedure: operative drainage into the anorectal lumen or <u>skin</u>  [[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)





> [!TIP]
> Uncomplicated <u>superficial</u> <u>abscesses</u> in otherwise healthy patients can be treated with <u>incision and drainage</u> in ambulatory settings. [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)




> [!WARNING]
> Consult <u>surgery</u> urgently for patients with <u>signs of sepsis</u>, extensive <u>cellulitis</u>, or comorbid risk-factors.




#### Adjunctive <u>antibiotics</u> [[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)




* Indications: signs of <u>cellulitis</u>, <u>signs of systemic infection</u> (e.g., <u>fever</u>), <u>immunosuppression</u>  [[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[7]](/library/b9WHNn0)

* Regimens: See “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for skin and soft tissue infections</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> In patients with <u>MDRO risk factors</u>, <u>immunosuppression</u>, and/or recurrent or non-healing <u>abscesses</u>, consider sampling drained <u>pus</u> and adjusting <u>antibiotic therapy</u> according to culture results. [[4]](/library/sDWtfn0)




#### Postsurgical care [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Sitz baths</u>

* <u>Analgesics</u> (e.g., <u>acetaminophen</u> or <u>NSAIDs</u>)

* <u>Stool softeners</u> and high-fiber diet to prevent <u>constipation</u>





> [!WARNING]
> All patients require postsurgical follow-up to ensure full resolution. Evaluate for <u>fistula</u> tracts if the <u>abscess</u> recurs or fails to resolve. [[6]](/library/OwWIQn0)




### <u>Fistulas</u> [[1]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[3]](/library/70a4hQ)




* Consult colorectal <u>surgery</u> for operative repair.

* Multiple surgical repair options exist, including: [[2]](/library/7DW4fn0)[[3]](/library/70a4hQ)

* Fistulotomy (standard approach)

* <u>Seton</u> placement

* Endorectal advancement <u>flap</u>

* Ligation of the intersphincteric <u>fistula</u> tract (LIFT)

* <u>Fistula</u> plug insertion

* <u>Fibrin</u> glue injection

* For patients with <u>Crohn disease</u>, see also “<u>Fistulizing Crohn disease</u>.”
